Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\n   516→\n   517→**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\n   518→- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\n   519→- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \n   520→- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \n   521→\n   522→**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers**\n   523→- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference papers\n   524→- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the papers's accuracy for each variable\n   525→- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \n   526→- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n   527→\n   528→**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n   529→- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n   530→\n   531→**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n   532→1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n   533→2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n   534→3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n   535→4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n   536→5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \n   537→\n   538→**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n   539→1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n   540→2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n   541→3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n   542→4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n   543→\n   544→**Report all checks and results** to `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n   545→\n   546→**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n   547→\n   548→---\n   549→\n   550→### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n   551→\n   552→**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n   553→\n   554→**Actions**:\n   555→- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n   556→  - Key decisions and rationale\n   557→  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n   558→  - Validation results and tables\n   559→  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n   560→- Create a user-facing `README.md` summarizing:\n   561→  - Dataset description\n   562→  - How to load and use the converted data\n   563→  - Output format specification\n   564→  - Key statistics\n   565→- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `cache/` folder\n   566→- Create `cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n   567→\n   568→**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n   569→\n   570→---\n   571→\n   572→## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n   573→\n   574→**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. Compute time bin indices\n   287→        time_bin_idx = np.floor((times_curr - t_beg) / BINSIZE).astype(np.int32)\n   288→        time_bin_idx = np.clip(time_bin_idx, 0, N_BINS - 1)\n   289→        \n   290→        # Use np.add.at for fast binning\n   291→        np.add.at(binned_all[trial_idx], (clust_curr, time_bin_idx), 1)\n   292→    \n   293→    return binned_all\n   294→\n   295→\n   296→def interpolate_behavior_to_bins(beh_times, beh_values, trial_starts, trial_ends):\n   297→    \"\"\"Interpolate continuous behavior signal to trial time bins.\n   298→    \n   299→    Returns array of shape (n_trials, n_bins).\n   300→    Matches get_behavior_per_interval from reference code.\n   301→    \"\"\"\n   302→    n_trials = len(trial_starts)\n   303→    result = np.full((n_trials, N_BINS), np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n   304→    valid = np.ones(n_trials, dtype=bool)\n   305→    \n   306→    for trial_idx in range(n_trials):\n   307→        t_beg = trial_starts[trial_idx]\n   308→        t_end = trial_ends[trial_idx]\n   309→        \n   310→        if np.isnan(t_beg) or np.isnan(t_end):\n   311→            valid[trial_idx] = False\n   312→            continue\n   313→        \n   314→        # Find behavior data in this interval\n   315→        idx_beg = np.searchsorted(beh_times, t_beg, side='right')\n   316→        idx_end = np.searchsorted(beh_times, t_end, side='left')\n   317→        \n   318→        beh_t = beh_times[idx_beg:idx_end]\n   319→        beh_v = beh_values[idx_beg:idx_end]\n   320→        \n   321→        if len(beh_v) < 2:\n   322→            valid[trial_idx] = False\n   323→            continue\n   324→        \n   325→        # Check for NaNs\n   326→        nan_mask = ~np.isnan(beh_v)\n   327→        if nan_mask.sum() < 2:\n   328→            valid[trial_idx] = False\n   329→            continue\n   330→        \n   331→        beh_t_clean = beh_t[nan_mask]\n   332→        beh_v_clean = beh_v[nan_mask]\n   333→        \n   334→        # Interpolate to uniform bins\n   335→        x_interp = np.linspace(t_beg, t_end, N_BINS, endpoint=False) + BINSIZE / 2\n   336→        \n   337→        try:\n   338→            y_interp = interpolate.interp1d(\n   339→                beh_t_clean, beh_v_clean, kind='linear',\n   340→                fill_value='extrapolate')(x_interp)\n   341→            result[trial_idx] = y_interp\n   342→        except Exception:\n   343→            valid[trial_idx] = False\n   344→    \n   345→    return result, valid\n   346→\n   347→\n   348→def discretize_time_varying(values, n_bins=N_DISC_BINS):\n   349→    \"\"\"Discretize continuous time-varying values into n_bins categories.\n   350→    \n   351→    Uses quantile-based binning across all timepoints in all trials.\n   352→    Returns integer categories 0, 1, ..., n_bins-1.\n   353→    \"\"\"\n   354→    # Flatten all values to compute quantiles\n   355→    flat = values[~np.isnan(values)].flatten()\n   356→    if len(flat) == 0:\n   357→        return np.zeros_like(values, dtype=np.int64)\n   358→    \n   359→    # Compute quantile boundaries\n   360→    quantiles = np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)[1:-1]\n   361→    boundaries = np.quantile(flat, quantiles)\n   362→    \n   363→    # Digitize\n   364→    result = np.digitize(values, boundaries).astype(np.int64)\n   365→    \n   366→    return result\n   367→\n   368→\n   369→def compute_trial_number_in_block(prob_left):\n   370→    \"\"\"Compute trial number within each block.\n   371→    \n   372→    Block changes when probabilityLeft changes.\n   373→    Trial number resets to 1 at each block change.\n   374→    \"\"\"\n   375→    trial_nums = np.zeros(len(prob_left), dtype=np.float32)\n   376→    counter = 1\n   377→    for i in range(len(prob_left)):\n   378→        if i > 0 and prob_left[i] != prob_left[i-1]:\n   379→            counter = 1\n   380→        trial_nums[i] = counter\n   381→        counter += 1\n   382→    return trial_nums\n   383→\n   384→\n   385→# ============================================================\n   386→# Main Processing\n   387→# ============================================================\n   388→\n   389→def process_session(session_info, session_dir, show_processing=False):\n   390→    \"\"\"Process a single session and return formatted data.\"\"\"\n   391→    eid = session_info['eid']\n   392→    lab = session_info['lab']\n   393→    subject = session_info['subject']\n   394→    date = session_info['date']\n   395→    probe_names = session_info['probe_names']\n   396→    \n   397→    t0 = time.time()\n   398→    \n   399→    # 1. Load trials\n   400→    trials_df = load_trials(session_dir)\n   401→    if trials_df is None:\n   402→        print(f\"  Skipping {eid}: no trials data\")\n   403→        return None\n   404→    \n   405→    # 2. Create trial mask\n   406→    mask = create_trials_mask(trials_df)\n   407→    \n   408→    # 3. Load spikes\n   409→    spike_times, spike_clusters, cluster_regions = load_spikes(session_dir, probe_names)\n   410→    if spike_times is None:\n   411→        print(f\"  Skipping {eid}: no spike data\")\n   412→        return None\n   413→    \n   414→    n_clusters = len(cluster_regions)\n   415→    \n   416→    # 4. Load wheel speed\n   417→    wheel_times, wheel_speed = load_wheel_speed(session_dir)\n   418→    has_wheel = wheel_times is not None\n   419→    \n   420→    # 5. Load whisker motion energy\n   421→    me_times, me_values = load_whisker_motion_energy(session_dir)\n   422→    has_me = me_times is not None\n   423→    \n   424→    # 6. Compute trial intervals (aligned to stimOn)\n   425→    stim_on = trials_df[ALIGN_TIME].values\n   426→    trial_starts = stim_on + TIME_WINDOW[0]\n   427→    trial_ends = stim_on + TIME_WINDOW[1]\n   428→    \n   429→    # 7. Bin spikes per trial (for ALL trials first, then filter)\n   430→    print(f\"  Binning spikes ({n_clusters} clusters, {len(trials_df)} trials)...\", end=' ')\n   431→    t_bin = time.time()\n   432→    binned_spikes = bin_spikes_per_trial(\n   433→        spike_times, spike_clusters, n_clusters, trial_starts, trial_ends)\n   434→    print(f\"{time.time()-t_bin:.1f}s\")\n   435→    \n   436→    # 8. Interpolate behaviors per trial\n   437→    if has_wheel:\n   438→        wheel_binned, wheel_valid = interpolate_behavior_to_bins(\n   439→            wheel_times, wheel_speed, trial_starts, trial_ends)\n   440→    else:\n   441→        wheel_valid = np.zeros(len(trials_df), dtype=bool)\n   442→    \n   443→    if has_me:\n   444→        me_binned, me_valid = interpolate_behavior_to_bins(\n   445→            me_times, me_values, trial_starts, trial_ends)\n   446→    else:\n   447→        me_valid = np.zeros(len(trials_df), dtype=bool)\n   448→    \n   449→    # 9. Combine masks: trial quality + behavior availability\n   450→    combined_mask = mask.values & wheel_valid & me_valid\n   451→    \n   452→    # Check we have enough trials\n   453→    n_valid = combined_mask.sum()\n   454→    if n_valid < 2:\n   455→        print(f\"  Skipping {eid}: only {n_valid} valid trials\")\n   456→        return None\n   457→    \n   458→    print(f\"  Valid trials: {n_valid}/{len(trials_df)} \"\n   459→          f\"(mask: {mask.sum()}, wheel: {wheel_valid.sum()}, me: {me_valid.sum()})\")\n   460→    \n   461→    # 10. Apply mask\n   462→    valid_idx = np.where(combined_mask)[0]\n   463→    neural_data = binned_spikes[valid_idx]  # (n_valid, n_clusters, N_BINS)\n   464→    \n   465→    # Get trial-level variables\n   466→    valid_trials = trials_df.iloc[valid_idx]\n   467→    \n   468→    # Choice: -1 -> 0 (left), 1 -> 1 (right)\n   469→    choice = valid_trials['choice'].values.copy()\n   470→    choice_mapped = np.where(choice == -1, 0, 1).astype(np.int64)\n   471→    \n   472→    # Prior: probabilityLeft 0.2->0, 0.5->1, 0.8->2\n   473→    prob_left = valid_trials['probabilityLeft'].values\n   474→    prior_map = {0.2: 0, 0.5: 1, 0.8: 2}\n   475→    prior_mapped = np.array([prior_map.get(p, 1) for p in prob_left], dtype=np.int64)\n   476→    \n   477→    # Trial number in block\n   478→    # Need to compute on ALL trials first, then select valid ones\n   479→    all_prob_left = trials_df['probabilityLeft'].values\n   480→    all_trial_nums = compute_trial_number_in_block(all_prob_left)\n   481→    trial_num_in_block = all_trial_nums[valid_idx]\n   482→    \n   483→    # Time since stimulus onset (same for all trials)\n   484→    time_since_stim = np.arange(N_BINS) * BINSIZE + TIME_WINDOW[0] + BINSIZE / 2\n   485→    time_since_stim = time_since_stim.astype(np.float32)\n   486→    \n   487→    # Wheel speed and whisker ME (already interpolated)\n   488→    wheel_data = wheel_binned[valid_idx]  # (n_valid, N_BINS)\n   489→    me_data = me_binned[valid_idx]  # (n_valid, N_BINS)\n   490→    \n   491→    # Discretize continuous outputs\n   492→    wheel_disc = discretize_time_varying(wheel_data, N_DISC_BINS)\n   493→    me_disc = discretize_time_varying(me_data, N_DISC_BINS)\n   494→    \n   495→    # Format output\n   496→    n_valid_trials = len(valid_idx)\n   497→    \n   498→    # Neural: list of (n_neurons, n_timepoints) arrays\n   499→    neural_list = [neural_data[i].astype(np.float32) for i in range(n_valid_trials)]\n   500→    \n   501→    # Input: list of (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input,) arrays\n   502→    # input[0] = time since stim onset (time-varying, same for all trials)\n   503→    # input[1] = trial number in block (per-trial)\n   504→    input_list = []\n   505→    for i in range(n_valid_trials):\n   506→        inp = np.vstack([\n   507→            time_since_stim[np.newaxis, :],  # (1, N_BINS)\n   508→            np.full((1, N_BINS), trial_num_in_block[i], dtype=np.float32)  # (1, N_BINS)\n   509→        ])  # (2, N_BINS)\n   510→        input_list.append(inp)\n   511→    \n   512→    # Output: list of (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output,) arrays\n   513→    # output[0] = choice (per-trial)\n   514→    # output[1] = prior (per-trial)\n   515→    # output[2] = wheel speed discretized (time-varying)\n   516→    # output[3] = whisker ME discretized (time-varying)\n   517→    output_list = []\n   518→    for i in range(n_valid_trials):\n   519→        out = np.vstack([\n   520→            np.full((1, N_BINS), choice_mapped[i], dtype=np.int64),  # (1, N_BINS)\n   521→            np.full((1, N_BINS), prior_mapped[i], dtype=np.int64),  # (1, N_BINS)\n   522→            wheel_disc[i:i+1, :],  # (1, N_BINS)\n   523→            me_disc[i:i+1, :],  # (1, N_BINS)\n   524→        ])  # (4, N_BINS)\n   525→        output_list.append(out)\n   526→    \n   527→    elapsed = time.time() - t0\n   528→    print(f\"  Session processed in {elapsed:.1f}s\")\n   529→    \n   530→    # Visualization\n   531→    if show_processing:\n   532→        plot_processing(session_dir, eid, trials_df, valid_idx, neural_data,\n   533→                       wheel_data, me_data, wheel_disc, me_disc,\n   534→                       choice_mapped, prior_mapped, time_since_stim)\n   535→    \n   536→    return {\n   537→        'neural': neural_list,\n   538→        'input': input_list,\n   539→        'output': output_list,\n   540→        'subject': subject,\n   541→        'cluster_regions': cluster_regions,\n   542→        'eid': eid,\n   543→        'n_trials': n_valid_trials,\n   544→        'n_neurons': n_clusters,\n   545→    }\n   546→\n   547→\n   548→def plot_processing(session_dir, eid, trials_df, valid_idx, neural_data,\n   549→                   wheel_data, me_data, wheel_disc, me_disc,\n   550→                   choice_mapped, prior_mapped, time_since_stim):\n   551→    \"\"\"Plot processing steps for visual verification.\"\"\"\n   552→    import matplotlib\n   553→    matplotlib.use('Agg')\n   554→    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n   555→    \n   556→    fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 3, figsize=(18, 16))\n   557→    fig.suptitle(f'Processing: {eid}', fontsize=14)\n   558→    \n   559→    # Select a few example trials\n   560→    n_examples = min(3, len(valid_idx))\n   561→    example_trials = np.random.choice(len(valid_idx), n_examples, replace=False)\n   562→    \n   563→    for col, trial_idx in enumerate(example_trials):\n   564→        # Row 0: Neural activity (raster of top neurons)\n   565→        ax = axes[0, col]\n   566→        n_show = min(50, neural_data.shape[1])\n   567→        ax.imshow(neural_data[trial_idx, :n_show, :], aspect='auto',\n   568→                  extent=[time_since_stim[0], time_since_stim[-1], n_show, 0])\n   569→        ax.set_title(f'Trial {valid_idx[trial_idx]}')\n   570→        ax.set_ylabel('Neuron' if col == 0 else '')\n   571→        ax.axvline(0, color='r', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)\n   572→        \n   573→        # Row 1: Wheel speed (continuous and discretized)\n   574→        ax = axes[1, col]\n   575→        ax.plot(time_since_stim, wheel_data[trial_idx], 'b-', alpha=0.7, label='continuous')\n   576→        ax2 = ax.twinx()\n   577→        ax2.plot(time_since_stim, wheel_disc[trial_idx], 'r-', alpha=0.5, label='discretized')\n   578→        ax.set_ylabel('Wheel speed' if col == 0 else '')\n   579→        ax.axvline(0, color='r', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)\n   580→        \n   581→        # Row 2: Whisker ME (continuous and discretized)\n   582→        ax = axes[2, col]\n   583→        ax.plot(time_since_stim, me_data[trial_idx], 'g-', alpha=0.7, label='continuous')\n   584→        ax2 = ax.twinx()\n   585→        ax2.plot(time_since_stim, me_disc[trial_idx], 'r-', alpha=0.5, label='discretized')\n   586→        ax.set_ylabel('Whisker ME' if col == 0 else '')\n   587→        ax.axvline(0, color='r', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)\n   588→        \n   589→        # Row 3: Choice and Prior\n   590→        ax = axes[3, col]\n   591→        ax.text(0.5, 0.7, f'Choice: {\"left\" if choice_mapped[trial_idx]==0 else \"right\"}',\n   592→                transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=12)\n   593→        ax.text(0.5, 0.3, f'Prior: {[\"0.2\",\"0.5\",\"0.8\"][prior_mapped[trial_idx]]}',\n   594→                transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=12)\n   595→        ax.set_xlabel('Time since stim onset (s)')\n   596→    \n   597→    plt.tight_layout()\n   598→    safe_eid = eid.replace('/', '_')\n   599→    plt.savefig(f'processing_{safe_eid}.png', dpi=150)\n   600→    plt.close()\n   601→    print(f\"  Saved processing plot: processing_{safe_eid}.png\")\n   602→\n   603→\n   604→def main():\n   605→    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Convert IBL BWM data to decoder format.')\n   606→    parser.add_argument('output', type=str, help='Output pickle file path')\n   607→    parser.add_argument('--full', action='store_true', default=True,\n   608→                       help='Process all sessions (default)')\n   609→    parser.add_argument('--sample', action='store_true',\n   610→                       help='Process only 2 sessions for testing')\n   611→    parser.add_argument('--show-processing', action='store_true',\n   612→                       help='Plot processing visualizations')\n   613→    args = parser.parse_args()\n   614→    \n   615→    if args.sample:\n   616→        args.full = False\n   617→    \n   618→    print(\"=\"*60)\n   619→    print(\"IBL BWM Data Conversion\")\n   620→    print(\"=\"*60)\n   621→    \n   622→    t_total = time.time()\n   623→    \n   624→    # Load session info from bwm_release.csv\n   625→    bwm_df = pd.read_csv('code/code_zhang2025/data/bwm_release.csv', index_col=0)\n   626→    \n   627→    # Group by eid to get session-level info with probe names\n   628→    session_groups = bwm_df.groupby('eid').agg({\n   629→        'lab': 'first',\n   630→        'subject': 'first',\n   631→        'date': 'first',\n   632→        'probe_name': list,\n   633→        'pid': list\n   634→    }).reset_index()\n   635→    session_groups.rename(columns={'probe_name': 'probe_names'}, inplace=True)\n   636→    \n   637→    print(f\"Total sessions in bwm_release: {len(session_groups)}\")\n   638→    \n   639→    if args.sample:\n   640→        # Select 2 sessions with complete data\n   641→        valid_sessions = []\n   642→        for _, row in session_groups.iterrows():\n   643→            session_dir = find_session_dir(row['lab'], row['subject'], row['date'])\n   644→            if session_dir is None:\n   645→                continue\n   646→            has_spikes = len(glob.glob(os.path.join(\n   647→                session_dir, 'alf', 'probe*', 'pykilosort', '*', 'spikes.times.npy'))) > 0\n   648→            has_trials = len(glob.glob(os.path.join(\n   649→                session_dir, 'alf', '*', '_ibl_trials.table.pqt'))) > 0\n   650→            has_wheel = os.path.exists(os.path.join(\n   651→                session_dir, 'alf', '_ibl_wheel.position.npy'))\n   652→            has_me = (find_file(session_dir, 'leftCamera.ROIMotionEnergy.npy') is not None and\n   653→                (find_file(session_dir, '_ibl_leftCamera.times.npy') is not None or\n   654→                 find_file(session_dir, '_ibl_rightCamera.times.npy') is not None)) or \\\n   655→                (find_file(session_dir, 'rightCamera.ROIMotionEnergy.npy') is not None and\n   656→                (find_file(session_dir, '_ibl_leftCamera.times.npy') is not None or\n   657→                 find_file(session_dir, '_ibl_rightCamera.times.npy') is not None))\n   658→            if has_spikes and has_trials and has_wheel and has_me:\n   659→                valid_sessions.append(row)\n   660→            if len(valid_sessions) >= 2:\n   661→                break\n   662→        session_groups = pd.DataFrame(valid_sessions)\n   663→        print(f\"Sample mode: processing {len(session_groups)} sessions\")\n   664→    \n   665→    # Process sessions\n   666→    all_neural = []\n   667→    all_input = []\n   668→    all_output = []\n   669→    all_subjects = []\n   670→    subject_idx_list = []\n   671→    all_brain_regions = []\n   672→    brain_region_idx_list = []\n   673→    session_eids = []\n   674→    \n   675→    subject_map = {}  # subject name -> index\n   676→    region_map = {}   # region name -> index\n   677→    \n   678→    n_processed = 0\n   679→    n_skipped = 0\n   680→    \n   681→    for sess_idx, (_, row) in enumerate(session_groups.iterrows()):\n   682→        eid = row['eid']\n   683→        lab = row['lab']\n   684→        subject = row['subject']\n   685→        date = row['date']\n   686→        probe_names = row['probe_names']\n   687→        \n   688→        print(f\"\\n[{sess_idx+1}/{len(session_groups)}] Processing {subject}/{date} ({eid})...\")\n   689→        \n   690→        session_dir = find_session_dir(lab, subject, date)\n   691→        if session_dir is None:\n   692→            print(f\"  Skipping: session directory not found\")\n   693→            n_skipped += 1\n   694→            continue\n   695→        \n   696→        session_info = {\n   697→            'eid': eid, 'lab': lab, 'subject': subject,\n   698→            'date': date, 'probe_names': probe_names\n   699→        }\n   700→        \n   701→        try:\n   702→            result = process_session(session_info, session_dir,\n   703→                                   show_processing=args.show_processing)\n   704→        except Exception as e:\n   705→            print(f\"  Error processing session: {e}\")\n   706→            import traceback\n   707→            traceback.print_exc()\n   708→            n_skipped += 1\n   709→            continue\n   710→        \n   711→        if result is None:\n   712→            n_skipped += 1\n   713→            continue\n   714→        \n   715→        # Add to lists\n   716→        all_neural.append(result['neural'])\n   717→        all_input.append(result['input'])\n   718→        all_output.append(result['output'])\n   719→        session_eids.append(result['eid'])\n   720→        \n   721→        # Subject mapping\n   722→        subj = result['subject']\n   723→        if subj not in subject_map:\n   724→            subject_map[subj] = len(all_subjects)\n   725→            all_subjects.append(subj)\n   726→        subject_idx_list.append(subject_map[subj])\n   727→        \n   728→        # Brain region mapping\n   729→        regions = result['cluster_regions']\n   730→        neuron_region_idx = np.zeros(len(regions), dtype=np.int64)\n   731→        for i, r in enumerate(regions):\n   732→            if r not in region_map:\n   733→                region_map[r] = len(all_brain_regions)\n   734→                all_brain_regions.append(r)\n   735→            neuron_region_idx[i] = region_map[r]\n   736→        brain_region_idx_list.append(neuron_region_idx)\n   737→        \n   738→        n_processed += 1\n   739→    \n   740→    print(f\"\\n{'='*60}\")\n   741→    print(f\"Processed: {n_processed} sessions, Skipped: {n_skipped}\")\n   742→    print(f\"Subjects: {len(all_subjects)}, Brain regions: {len(all_brain_regions)}\")\n   743→    \n   744→    if n_processed == 0:\n   745→        print(\"ERROR: No sessions processed!\")\n   746→        sys.exit(1)\n   747→    \n   748→    # {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01G7VWxTGTari7tw5nxQukKX","type":"tool_result","content":"     1→From \"Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding\"\n     2→\n     3→Our goal is to decode behavior y \\in R^P from spike-sorted, temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \\in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \\in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).\n     4→\n     5→We apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.\n     6→\n     7→ In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\n     8→\n     9→Data processing\n    10→\n    11→IBL trial-aligned dataset\n    12→\n    13→For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\n    14→\n    15→IBL trial-unaligned dataset\n    16→\n    17→We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.\n    18→\n    19→From \"A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour\"\n    20→\n    21→We trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\n    22→\n    23→Recordings\n    24→\n    25→In these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\n    26→\n    27→Methods\n    28→\n    29→n brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\n    30→\n    31→Each session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \\in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \\in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).\n\nWe apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.\n\n In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\n\nData processing\n\nIBL trial-aligned dataset\n\nFor choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\n\nIBL trial-unaligned dataset\n\nWe focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\n\nRecordings\n\nIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\n\nMethods\n\nn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\n\nEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Some data may be missing and may need to be downloaded. \\n- **Documentation** about how to access the data can be found at https://docs.internationalbrainlab.org/public_docs/public_introduction.html.\\n\\n## Decoder Task\\n\\nTemporally align based on stimulus onset\\n\\n### Decoder Inputs:\\n- Time since stimulus onset, continuous, time-varying\\n- Trial number in block, continuous, per-trial\\n\\n### Decoder Outputs\\n- Choice, binary, per-trial, left = 0, right = 1\\n- Prior probability of left, per-trial, 0.2 -> 0, 0.5 -> 1, 0.8 -> 2\\n- Wheel speed discretized into 3 bins, time-varying\\n- Whisker motion energy discretized into 3 bins, time-varying\\n\\n## Target Data Format\\n\\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `converted_data.pkl`.\\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\\n\\n```python\\ndata = {\\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\\n\\n### Consistency requirements\\n\\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\\n- Loading of data\\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\\n\\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \\n\\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \\n\\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above. \\n\\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \\n\\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \\n\\n---\\n\\n## Conversion Workflow\\n\\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \\n\\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \\n\\n---\\n\\n## Conversion Workflow\\n\\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. Each step has explicit completion criteria. Do not proceed to the next step until the current step is complete. Use the exact step names below when documenting progress in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n**STATUS TRACKING**: At the start of each step, update its status to `IN PROGRESS` in CONVERSION_NOTES.md. When complete, update to `COMPLETE`. This helps you and the user track progress.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 0: Setup and Initialization\\n\\n**Goal**: Set up the working environment and create the notes file.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. **FIRST**: Create `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` with the template structure shown at the end of this document\\n2. Verify you can run `python3` and import key packages (numpy, torch)\\n3. List the contents of this directory to understand what files are available\\n4. **REMINDER**: Do NOT look at any files outside this directory\\n\\n**Done when**: \\n- `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` exists with the proper template structure\\n- You have confirmed Python and key packages work\\n- You have listed directory contents in CONVERSION_NOTES.md\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 1, verify that `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` exists by running `ls -la CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. If it doesn't exist, STOP and create it now.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 1: Reference Code Exploration\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CONSTRAINT REMINDER**: Only look at code in the `code` directory. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\\n\\n**Goal**: Understand how the original authors loaded and processed their data.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Look for documentation or README files in the `code` directory\\n- Read the provided reference code bases to see how the reference paper loaded and manipulated the data\\n- Understand which functions are being called to read, curate, process, and manipulate the data\\n- For neural imaging data, does delta F over F need to be computed? \\n- For electrophysiology neural data, do cells need to be filtered based on quality? \\n- Note to file important functions, their inputs, and outputs\\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented key functions and their purposes in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 1\\\".\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 2, update Step 1 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 2: Dataset Exploration\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CONSTRAINT REMINDER**: Only look at data in the `data` directory. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\\n\\n**Goal**: Understand the native data structure\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Identify how data is organized (all files, formats, hierarchies)\\n- Determine available variables and their meanings\\n- Check data dimensions and data types\\n- Look for documentation or README files\\n- Note the data organization and structure\\n- Note dataset size parameters such as the **total number** of subjects (mice), sessions, trials, and neurons\\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented the data structure, file formats, size, and available variables in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 2\\\".\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 3, update Step 2 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 3: Reference Text Reading\\n\\n**Goal**: Extract key information from the paper and methods.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Scan the reference papers and methods.txt for important details about the data\\n- Look for and note to file:\\n  - Any information about dataset size (number of neurons, subjects, sessions, trials)\\n  - Fraction of data with different values, e.g. fraction of rewarded outcomes\\n  - Data processing, curation, and filtering\\n  - Variables important to experiments\\n  - Temporal alignment\\n  - Temporal binning\\n- Read the reference paper to find information about expected decoder accuracy.\\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented expected dataset statistics and processing details in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 3\\\".\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 4, update Step 3 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 4: Check for Consistency\\n\\n**Goal**: Verify your understanding is consistent across all sources. \\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Compare your understanding of:\\n  - Important functions from exploring the reference code\\n  - Dataset structure from exploring the dataset\\n  - Analysis described in the reference texts\\n- Note and investigate any discrepancies\\n- In particular, look for discrepancies in:\\n  - Experimental and behavioral variables\\n  - Data processing\\n  - Data curation\\n- Iterate until your understanding of the reference code, dataset, and reference texts are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**: You have resolved all discrepancies and documented your final understanding in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 4\\\".\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 5, update Step 4 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 5: Mapping Planning\\n\\n**Goal**: Create a detailed plan for mapping source data to target format.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Map source data elements to target format components:\\n  - Which variables contain neural activity?\\n  - Identify ALL available experimental variables\\n  - Which variables should be decoder **inputs** vs **outputs**? (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - How to discretize continuous outputs (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - Which inputs/outputs should be **time-varying** vs **per-trial** (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - How does the reference code load and manipulate this data?\\n  - When possible, import or copy code from the reference code in `code` directory. \\n- Consult CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4 and reference materials to determine:\\n  - Temporal binning for spike rates (if applicable)\\n  - Temporal alignment of trials\\n  - Data filtering and curation rules for neurons, trials, and sessions\\n  - Brain regions recorded from\\n- Mapping should be consistent with CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4.\\n- Check for variables indicating valid data periods \\u2014 exclude invalid data\\n- Note all decisions, edge cases, and data quality issues\\n- Plan and document **sanity and consistency checks** based on dataset size information from the reference texts, code, and data\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- You have a complete mapping document in CONVERSION_NOTES.md specifying every source-to-target variable mapping under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n- You have documented all decisions under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n- You have documented sanity and consistency checks under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 6, update Step 5 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 6: Script Development\\n\\n**Goal**: Write the conversion script to `convert_data.py`.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Write all conversion code in the file `convert_data.py`\\n- Script should run as **`python -u convert_data.py <outpicklefile>`**\\n- Include options:\\n  - `--full` (default): Process all sessions\\n  - `--sample`: Process only 2 sessions for testing\\n  - `--show-processing`: Plot visualizations of EVERY processing step for up to 2 sessions. Save plots as `processing_<session_id>.png`.\\n- Reuse code from reference code bases where appropriate\\n- Write efficient code:\\n  - Vectorize loops\\n  - Avoid unnecessary file I/O\\n  - Use parallel processing if beneficial\\n  - Print timing information to find bottlenecks\\n- Plots for `--show-processing` mode should visually convince the user that every step of the conversion is correct.\\n  - There are no temporal misalignments\\n  - Discretization of continuous outputs is correct\\n- Write clear, well-documented functions\\n- Handle missing data appropriately (consult references, use sensible defaults, document)\\n- Validate data shapes and types at each step\\n- Include sanity checks (e.g., trial counts match across arrays)\\n\\n**Done when**: `convert_data.py` exists and runs efficiently without errors.\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 7 until `convert_data.py` exists and you have updated Step 6 in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the conversion on a small sample before processing the full dataset.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u convert_data.py sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee conversion_sample_out.txt`\\n  a. Verify the sample data structure matches the specification.\\n  b. Check dimensions are consistent across trials/sessions.\\n  c. Check that no data is missed during conversion. \\n  d. Validate that metadata accurately describes the data.\\n2. Improve efficiency of conversion.\\n  a. Look at and note timing information for the conversion. \\n  b. Estimate how long the full conversion will run. When you do this, make sure that your estimate accounts for differences in lengths/numbers of trials/sessions. \\n  c. If full conversion time estimate is longer than 15 minutes, speed up the code by writing more efficient code (vectorizing loops, removing unnecessary or redundant computations) and/or including parallel processing. \\n3. Run `python -u train_decoder.py sample_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee verification_sample_out.txt`.\\n4. Analyze the output file `verification_sample_out.txt`:\\n  a. Verify no errors reported.\\n  b. Attempt to address any warnings\\n  c. Check input ranges and output value distributions against expectations from reference texts.\\n\\n**Done when**: \\n- `sample_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `verification_sample_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- Processing plots show no anomalies\\n- Document sample statistics in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 7\\\"\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 8 until `sample_data.pkl` and `verification_sample_out.txt` files exist, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 7 is filled in. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 8: Sample Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Verify the decoder runs successfully on sample data.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u train_decoder.py sample_data.pkl 2>&1 | tee train_decoder_sample_out.txt`\\n2. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\\n3. **Check accuracy**: Verify accuracy is above chance for EVERY output\\n\\n**Investigate any issues**:\\n- If accuracy is low: check for conversion bugs or reconsider output representation\\n\\n**Done when**: \\n- Decoder training completes without errors\\n- Loss decreases over epochs\\n- Accuracies are above chance\\n- Document all results in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 8\\\"\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 9 until `train_decoder_sample_out.txt` file exists, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 8 is filled in. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 9: Full Conversion and Validation\\n\\n**Goal**: Process the complete dataset.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Review your time estimate from Step 7.\\n2. If estimated time is long (e.g. longer than 15 minutes), optimize bottlenecks first.\\n3. Run `python -u convert_data.py converted_data.pkl --full 2>&1 | tee conversion_full_out.txt`\\n4. As the code runs, update your estimates of how long processing will take. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \\n5. Run `python -u train_decoder.py converted_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee verification_full_out.txt`. \\n6. Check that no data was lost during conversion \\n7. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\\n8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\\n9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- `converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\\n- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 9\\\"\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `converted_data.pkl` and `verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 10: Critical Review 1\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain.\\n\\n**Check 1: Output log verification**\\nRead through `verification_full_out.txt` to find and fix **all errors**. Address each warning by either fixing its cause or verifying it that it is not possible to fix it. Explain why each warning could not be fixed in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 2: Construct sanity checks**\\n- Develop at least one sanity check each on neural, input, and output data.\\n- These must involve loading in the original data files (NOT through your conversion code).\\n- Construct comparison tests and criteria using `np.allclose()`. \\n- These tests can be spot-checks of the data, e.g. neural activity at trial 5, timepoint 10, neuron 3. \\n- Fix all mismatches/sanity check failures. \\n- Document your sanity checks to `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 3: Reference code comparison**\\n- Compare your code to the reference code and methods. \\n- For each major processing step \\u2014 (a) data loading, (b) neuron/trial filtering, (c) temporal alignment, (d) binning, (e) input construction, (f) output construction \\u2014 identify the corresponding code in your script and in the reference, and compare the logic. \\n- Check whether you use the same variables, filtering, and processing as the reference code. \\n- Fix any mismatches. \\n- Document your comparisons in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n- Explain your reasoning for any differences in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`.\\n\\n**Check 4: Key statistics comparison**\\n- Verify that key statistics (number of animals, sessions, trials, neurons, input and output ranges, output distributions) match information available in the reference papers. \\n- Write code to investigate any discrepancies. \\n- Fix any discovered issues. \\n- Document your comparisons in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 5: Check for edge cases**\\n- Check for off-by-one errors at the beginning/ends of trials, sessions, and subjects, or in definitions of the inputs and outputs. \\n- There may be minor issues in the data that your code must handle. Check that your code robustly handles issues in the original data. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\nWrite a report to CONVERSION_NOTES.md describing **every** check you did, to help convince the user that the conversion code works. **Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 10\\\".\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 11 until you have checked for consistency between **every** statistic in the reference texts, code, and data and documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Step 10. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 11: Full Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the decoder on the **complete** dataset.\\n\\n**\\u26a0\\ufe0f IMPORTANT**: This step must complete fully. Do not skip or abbreviate. Do not proceed to Step 12 until this step is completely finished.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u train_decoder.py converted_data.pkl --plot-samples 2>&1 | tee train_decoder_full_out.txt`. If the GPU does not have sufficient RAM for the network training, use the flag `--cpu` to specify to use the CPU to train. \\n2. **Wait for complete execution** \\u2014 this may take significant time for large datasets\\n3. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\\n4. **Check accuracy**: High accuracy is an indicator that data conversion has been done correctly. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the papers. \\n\\n**Done when**: \\n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 11\\\" with a table of accuracies\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\\n\\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \\n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \\n\\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers**\\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference papers\\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the papers's accuracy for each variable\\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \\n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \\n\\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \\n\\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\\n2. Check temporal alignment \\u2014 plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \\n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\n**Report all checks and results** to `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 12\\\".\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\\n\\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\\n  - Key decisions and rationale\\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\\n  - Validation results and tables\\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\\n- Create a user-facing `README.md` summarizing:\\n  - Dataset description\\n  - How to load and use the converted data\\n  - Output format specification\\n  - Key statistics\\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `cache/` folder\\n- Create `cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\\n\\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\\n\\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. Match the target data structure exactly\\n2. Preserve all relevant information from the source\\n3. Have consistent dimensions across trials/sessions\\n4. The AI applies several filters via `create_trials_mask()`:\n- Reaction time (firstMovement_times - stimOn_times) must be between 0.08s and 2.0s\n- Trial length (feedback_times - goCue_times) must be <= 10.0s\n- No NaN in: stimOn_times, choice, feedback_times, probabilityLeft, firstMovement_times, feedbackType\n- Exclude no-choice trials (choice == 0)\n- Additionally, trials must have valid wheel and whisker motion energy data (at least 2 non-NaN interpolation points)\n\nii.\n```python\ndef create_trials_mask(trials_df):\n    nan_exclude = ['stimOn_times', 'choice', 'feedback_times',\n                   'probabilityLeft', 'firstMovement_times', 'feedbackType']\n    mask = pd.Series(True, index=trials_df.index)\n    rt = trials_df['firstMovement_times'] - trials_df['stimOn_times']\n    if MIN_RT is not None:\n        mask &= (rt >= MIN_RT)\n    if MAX_RT is not None:\n        mask &= (rt <= MAX_RT)\n    if MAX_TRIAL_LEN is not None:\n        trial_len = trials_df['feedback_times'] - trials_df['goCue_times']\n        mask &= (trial_len <= MAX_TRIAL_LEN)\n    for event in nan_exclude:\n        if event in trials_df.columns:\n            mask &= ~trials_df[event].isna()\n    mask &= (trials_df['choice'] != 0)\n    return mask\n# Later combined:\ncombined_mask = mask.values & wheel_valid & me_valid\n```\n\niii. The CONVERSION_NOTES.md documents these criteria under Step 1 and Step 3, matching `load_trials_and_mask()` from the reference code. The reference code uses the same default parameters: min_rt=0.08, max_rt=2.0, max_trial_len=10.0, exclude_nochoice=True, and the same nan_exclude list.\n\n## 2-a. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times and cluster IDs from multiple probes are merged (with cluster ID offsets to avoid collisions), sorted by time, then binned into 20ms time bins within each trial's time window. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time since stimulus onset*?\n\ni. A linearly spaced array of bin center times is computed. Each value equals the bin start time plus half the bin width. This is a straightforward computation. The same time array is shared across all trials as the alignment is always to stimOn_times.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time since stimulus onset* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The time since stimulus onset array and the neural data share the same 100-bin temporal structure by construction. Bin `i` of the neural data and bin `i` of the time input correspond to the same time window `[TIME_WINDOW[0] + i*BINSIZE, TIME_WINDOW[0] + (i+1)*BINSIZE]`. The input is broadcast to shape `(1, N_BINS)` for each trial.\n\nii.\n```python\ninp = np.vstack([\n    time_since_stim[np.newaxis, :],  # (1, N_BINS)\n    np.full((1, N_BINS), trial_num_in_block[i], dtype=np.float32)\n])\n```\n\niii. The AI iterates through all trials in order. A counter starts at 1 and increments for each trial. When `probabilityLeft` changes compared to the previous trial, the counter resets to 1. The computation is done on ALL trials first (including excluded ones), then valid trial indices are selected. The value is broadcast to all time bins within a trial.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_trial_number_in_block(prob_left):\n    trial_nums = np.zeros(len(prob_left), dtype=np.float32)\n    counter = 1\n    for i in range(len(prob_left)):\n        if i > 0 and prob_left[i] != prob_left[i-1]:\n            counter = 1\n        trial_nums[i] = counter\n        counter += 1\n    return trial_nums\n```\n\niii. For each trial, we constructed X \\in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \\in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).\n\nWe apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.\n\n In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions.
